abstract: Reliable deployment of LLM agents requires grounding diverse user expressions in their environments. Although RL-finetuned smaller large language model (sLLM) agents rival larger prompted LLMs on embodied tasks, their robustness to instruction paraphrases remains unclear. We introduce ALFWorld-Para to evaluate this robustness under controlled paraphrases, revealing 21–52% declines in success rates (SRs), predominantly driven by object synonyms. Despite retaining knowledge of synonym referents, agents often fail to take the corresponding objects even after observing them, exposing a gap between referential knowledge and object binding. Partial observability further complicates binding, as referents may remain unseen or have already been encountered under different labels. To address this challenge, we propose BINDIntent, a training-free framework that probabilistically binds referring expressions to observed labels using semantic proximity and estimated persistence against unseen candidates. Without additional training or LLM calls, BINDIntent improves synonym-paraphrase success of RL-finetuned sLLMs by 17.5–49.1 percentage points (pp) with only 0.4 ms of CPU overhead per step. It also raises GiGPO-7B’s overall SR from 61.8% to 77.4%, surpassing a prompted 24B LLM. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/cau-hai-lab/ALFWorld-Para.

sections.body: The introduction motivates robustness to instruction paraphrases for small language model agents trained with reinforcement learning, which can rival larger prompted models on embodied tasks. The authors build ALFWorld-Para, which varies only goal phrasing and paraphrases action and object expressions independently. RL-finetuned agents and prompted LLMs show 21–52% declines in success rate, and the RL-finetuned 7B models identify the corresponding labels with nearly 80% accuracy. The proposed BINDIntent is a training-free framework that binds referring expressions to observed labels using embedding distance and estimated persistence, adding about 0.4 ms of CPU overhead per step. On RL-finetuned sLLMs it improves synonym-paraphrase success by 17.5–49.1 pp and overall success by 7.0–20.6 pp.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Paraphrased instructions lower success of reinforcement-learning-tuned small agents, and a training-free binding method partly recovers it.

sections.body: The related work traces LLM agents from prompting and supervised fine-tuning to reinforcement learning, with algorithms including PPO, GRPO, GiGPO and StraTA. It notes that RL-finetuned small agents can outperform larger prompted LLMs, yet they are evaluated on the same instruction templates used in training. Table 1 shows that existing robustness studies focus on system-side perturbations such as prompt templates, action interfaces, environment configurations and model parameters. Prior RL studies each evaluate a single RL algorithm, and their mitigations require additional training. Grounding methods either rely on responsive users or assume all candidate actions are available upfront. The authors evaluate 29 paraphrase types across five prompted LLMs and agents fine-tuned with four RL algorithms, and propose a training-free mitigation.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior robustness studies focus on system-side perturbations, leaving paraphrased user instructions for RL-finetuned agents largely unexamined.

sections.body: ALFWorld goal instructions come from predefined templates, so ALFWorld-Para adapts the LIBERO-Para taxonomy to 226 unique goal instructions from the seen split. Action and object expressions are varied along separate axes, yielding 29 paraphrase types and 6,554 paraphrased instructions. The evaluation covers RL-finetuned Qwen2.5-1.5B and 7B agents trained with PPO, GRPO, GiGPO and StraTA, and five pretrained LLMs prompted with ReAct. All models degrade, with relative SR drops of 21–52%. GiGPO-7B leads Qwen3-14B by 13.7 pp on ALFWorld (95.8 vs. 82.1) but by only 1.7 pp on ALFWorld-Para (61.8 vs. 60.1). StraTA-1.5B has the highest original SR among 1.5B models but suffers a 41.9% relative drop. Even Mistral-Small-3-24B shows a 20.9% relative drop.
sections.heading: ALFWorld-Para
sections.headline: Paraphrased goals cut success 21–52% relative, and RL-finetuned small models lose their edge over larger prompted models.

sections.body: The first analysis finds that Same-Polarity object synonyms collapse success for RL-finetuned sLLMs, while Addition causes only minor drops. Action paraphrases other than Question and Hint keep success comparable to the original instructions. The referential knowledge probe tests whether models match a synonym to its original label, with chance level at 1.2%. RL-finetuned 7B models reach nearly 80% paraphrase knowledge, so the knowledge needed for the task is largely preserved. The taken-rate analysis then shows that under Same-Polarity, agents take the target object far less often even when they have observed it, and some 7B algorithms fall below the backbone at 41.3%. The authors conclude that failures come from binding paraphrased expressions to encountered objects rather than from knowledge loss.
sections.heading: Analysis
sections.headline: Object synonyms drive most failures, and agents often fail to take objects they already observed under synonyms.

sections.body: The method treats binding as uncertainty about objects not yet observed. Candidate labels within a lexical allowance are scored with ConceptNet Numberbatch cosine distance after removing the mean embedding of the observed labels, and the closest observed label becomes the best match. Observed distances are modeled with a Weibull distribution to estimate the probability that an unseen candidate is farther than the best match. Treating each unexplored unit as one candidate opportunity gives persistence $P_t=p_t^{k_t}$. Binding is cumulative, so the probability of binding equals the running maximum of persistence, and a Bernoulli trial decides binding at each step. Once bound, the slot is replaced with the current best match before the frozen agent receives the instruction. The method requires no training and no LLM calls.
sections.heading: Proposed Method
sections.headline: BINDIntent binds paraphrased object expressions to observed labels by embedding distance and estimated persistence against unseen candidates.

sections.body: BINDIntent is compared with a baseline that leaves grounding to the LLM, with Greedy binding, with self-clarification, and with a variant using general-purpose sentence embeddings. BINDIntent improves Same-Polarity success by 17.5–49.1 pp over the baseline for RL-finetuned sLLMs, while the None condition varies by at most 3 pp. Greedy binding lowers success on unchanged objects, for example GiGPO-7B None falls from 89.2 to 62.5. Self-clarification makes an agent LLM call per decision and underperforms the baseline on all 1.5B models. Per-step cost is 0.38 ms for BINDIntent against 0.25 ms for Greedy. On ScienceWorld-Para, BINDIntent improves Same-Polarity success by 7.0–10.2 pp, and the authors note that base models gain little because their original success is low.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: BINDIntent raises GiGPO-7B overall success to 77.4, surpassing prompted Mistral-Small-3-24B.

sections.body: The conclusion states that paraphrase failures arise from referent binding under partial observability rather than from knowledge loss. Such failures are missed by fully observable probes and emerge during execution, when agents must distinguish unseen referents from previously encountered objects. The authors argue that template-based benchmarks and knowledge probes alone may not capture this vulnerability. They call for principled reasoning about unobserved referents without compromising sLLM efficiency, rather than relying solely on fine-tuning or model scaling. BINDIntent is presented as evidence for this direction, recovering substantial performance through training-free probabilistic binding.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Paraphrase failures stem from referent binding under partial observability, not knowledge loss, so fine-tuning alone may not suffice.

sections.body: The limitations state that the work focuses on binding failures caused by object synonym substitutions, which show the most pronounced degradation. Whether BINDIntent applies to other paraphrase types, particularly action-axis variations such as Question and Hint, remains to be investigated. BINDIntent operates on observed objects without modifying the agent's exploration policy. The influence of exploration behaviors, which may vary across RL-finetuned agents, has not been systematically isolated. The authors suggest that future work could integrate binding with exploration strategies to find relevant objects.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: The method targets synonym-driven binding failures, leaving action-axis paraphrases and the exploration policy unaddressed.

sections.body: The appendix describes the paraphrase taxonomy and the factored generation pipeline using Gemini 3 Flash, with prompts and verifiers shown in figures. Parser stability is reported as 99.8% of 13,108 gold slots recovered. In the human evaluation, 324 of 328 pairs (98.8%) were judged meaning-preserving under majority vote, and 319 of 328 (97.3%) preserve the original task semantics after adjudication. Table 7 lists the codebase and weights used for each model, and the same paraphrased instructions are given to every codebase. Further sections report ScienceWorld-Para results, including paraphrase knowledge, taken rates, and per-step latency. The appendix also discloses the use of AI assistants.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers benchmark generation, human equivalence checks, codebases, extra per-type results, and ScienceWorld-Para analyses.
